**Status:** Phase 0 formal design  
**Scope:** Total, pure, variable-free presentation of the free bicartesian closed category generated by a signature

---

## 1. Purpose

This document defines the syntax, typing, definitional equality, checking boundary, simplification interface, and executable interpretation interface of the Phase 0 core.

The associated categorical construction, universal properties, models, and Lean theorem requirements are specified in [[Projects/CategoryLanguage/Metatheory and Categorical Semantics|Metatheory and Categorical Semantics]].

The kernel is intentionally smaller than the intended source language.

It contains no:

- Variables
- Local bindings
- Source lambdas
- Pattern syntax
- Alias declarations
- User-defined polymorphism
- Recursive types
- Effects
- Resource-sensitive values
- Concurrency
- Built-in arithmetic laws

The kernel provides the trusted categorical foundation into which later language features elaborate.

---

- Evaluation

- Sound categorical simplification

Phase 0 excludes:

- Source parsing
- Alias declarations
- Variables
- Local bindings
- Source lambdas
- Pattern syntax
- User-defined polymorphism
- Recursive data
- General recursion
- Algebraic effects

---

## 3. Notation

A morphism from `A` to `B` is written:

```text
A ⟶ B
```

The exponential object is written:

```text
A ⇒ B
```

Composition reads left to right:

```text
f >>> g
```

means “run `f`, then run `g`.”

If:

```text
f : A ⟶ B
g : B ⟶ C
```

then:

```text
f >>> g : A ⟶ C
```

---

## 4. Signatures

A Phase 0 kernel is instantiated with a finite or otherwise decidable resolved signature `Σ`.

A signature contains:

1. A collection of base-object identities.
2. A collection of generating-morphism identities.
3. A declared source and target object for each generator.

Example source notation:

```text
base Number

generator two   : Unit ⟶ Number
generator three : Unit ⟶ Number
generator add   : Number × Number ⟶ Number
```

After signature construction, names are resolved into typed internal identities.

Generators are opaque atomic leaves.

The kernel assumes no additional equations between them.

---

## 5. Object Grammar

Given `Σ`, core objects are generated by:

```text
A, B ::= Base(id)
       | Unit
       | Never
       | A × B
       | A + B
       | A ⇒ B
```

`Base(id)` is valid only when `id` belongs to `Σ`.

### 5.1 Structural equality

Object equality is structural within one signature context.

Two objects are equal exactly when:

- They have the same constructor.
- Corresponding children are structurally equal.
- Base objects have the same resolved identity.

These remain distinct:

```text
(A × B) × C
A × (B × C)

A × B
B × A

A × Unit
A

A + Never
A
```

### 5.2 Chosen structure

The syntax chooses concrete representatives for:

- `Unit`
- `Never`
- `A × B`
- `A + B`
- `A ⇒ B`

Canonical isomorphisms are explicit morphisms.

They are not definitional object equalities.

### 5.3 Aliases

Aliases are not core syntax.

```text
alias Bool = Unit + Unit
```

elaborates to:

```text
Unit + Unit
```

before the kernel receives the object.

### 5.4 Nominal objects

Nominal source-language types elaborate into distinct base objects.

Runtime representation sharing does not imply core equality.

---

## 6. Derived Boolean Object

The standard Boolean alias is:

```text
Bool = Unit + Unit
```

Its values are:

```text
false : Unit ⟶ Bool
false = left[Unit, Unit]

true : Unit ⟶ Bool
true = right[Unit, Unit]
```

Boolean elimination is coproduct elimination.

No Boolean primitive exists in the kernel.

---

## 7. Explicit Core Terms

Resolved explicit terms are generated by:

```text
t, u ::= generator[q]
       | id[A]
       | t >>> u
       | discard[A]
       | absurd[A]
       | first[A, B]
       | second[A, B]
       | pair(t, u)
       | left[A, B]
       | right[A, B]
       | case(t, u)
       | curry(t)
       | eval[A, B]
```

A `Term` is:

- Structurally valid
- Fully resolved under one signature
- Free of names requiring lookup
- Potentially categorically ill typed

A `Term` is not yet a trusted morphism.

---

## 8. Checked Morphisms

A successful checking judgment:

```text
Σ ⊢ t : A ⟶ B
```

produces a trusted checked morphism:

```text
f : A ⟶ B
```

Every checked subtree stores its exact source and target.

Only the checker and trusted internal constructors may create checked morphisms.

---

## 9. Typing Rules

### Generators

If `Σ` declares:

```text
q : A ⟶ B
```

then:

```text
Σ ⊢ generator[q] : A ⟶ B
```

### Identity

```text
Σ ⊢ id[A] : A ⟶ A
```

### Composition

If:

```text
Σ ⊢ t : A ⟶ B
Σ ⊢ u : B ⟶ C
```

then:

```text
Σ ⊢ t >>> u : A ⟶ C
```

No implicit conversion is inserted.

### Terminal elimination

```text
Σ ⊢ discard[A] : A ⟶ Unit
```

### Initial elimination

```text
Σ ⊢ absurd[A] : Never ⟶ A
```

### Product projections

```text
Σ ⊢ first[A, B]  : A × B ⟶ A
Σ ⊢ second[A, B] : A × B ⟶ B
```

### Product pairing

If:

```text
Σ ⊢ t : X ⟶ A
Σ ⊢ u : X ⟶ B
```

then:

```text
Σ ⊢ pair(t, u) : X ⟶ A × B
```

### Coproduct injections

```text
Σ ⊢ left[A, B]  : A ⟶ A + B
Σ ⊢ right[A, B] : B ⟶ A + B
```

### Coproduct elimination

If:

```text
Σ ⊢ t : A ⟶ X
Σ ⊢ u : B ⟶ X
```

then:

```text
Σ ⊢ case(t, u) : A + B ⟶ X
```

### Currying

If:

```text
Σ ⊢ t : X × A ⟶ B
```

then:

```text
Σ ⊢ curry(t) : X ⟶ A ⇒ B
```

### Evaluation

```text
Σ ⊢ eval[A, B] : (A ⇒ B) × A ⟶ B
```

---

## 10. Derived Morphisms

Derived definitions do not expand the trusted kernel.

### Uncurrying

For:

```text
k : X ⟶ A ⇒ B
```

define:

```text
uncurry(k) =
    pair(
        first[X, A] >>> k,
        second[X, A]
    )
    >>> eval[A, B]
```

with:

```text
uncurry(k) : X × A ⟶ B
```

### Product swap

```text
swapProduct[A, B] =
    pair(
        second[A, B],
        first[A, B]
    )
```

### Coproduct swap

```text
swapCoproduct[A, B] =
    case(
        right[B, A],
        left[B, A]
    )
```

### Reassociation

Product and coproduct reassociation are explicit derived isomorphisms.

### Unit and initial-object isomorphisms

Morphisms connecting:

```text
A × Unit
A
```

and:

```text
A + Never
A
```

are explicit derived morphisms.

---

## 11. Definitional Equality

The judgment:

```text
Σ ⊢ f ≡ g : A ⟶ B
```

means that `f` and `g` denote the same morphism in the free bicartesian closed category generated by `Σ`.

Opaque generators have no equations beyond those forced by the bicartesian-closed structure.

---

## 12. Category Laws

### Left identity

```text
id[A] >>> f ≡ f
```

### Right identity

```text
f >>> id[B] ≡ f
```

### Associativity

```text
(f >>> g) >>> h
≡
f >>> (g >>> h)
```

---

## 13. Terminal and Initial Laws

For every:

```text
f : A ⟶ Unit
```

```text
f ≡ discard[A]
```

For every:

```text
f : Never ⟶ A
```

```text
f ≡ absurd[A]
```

---

## 14. Product Laws

For:

```text
f : X ⟶ A
g : X ⟶ B
h : X ⟶ A × B
```

### Beta

```text
pair(f, g) >>> first[A, B]
≡
f
```

```text
pair(f, g) >>> second[A, B]
≡
g
```

### Eta

```text
pair(
    h >>> first[A, B],
    h >>> second[A, B]
)
≡
h
```

---

## 15. Coproduct Laws

For:

```text
f : A ⟶ X
g : B ⟶ X
h : A + B ⟶ X
```

### Beta

```text
left[A, B] >>> case(f, g)
≡
f
```

```text
right[A, B] >>> case(f, g)
≡
g
```

### Eta

```text
case(
    left[A, B] >>> h,
    right[A, B] >>> h
)
≡
h
```

The equality relation includes all consequences under congruence and composition, including necessary commuting conversions.

---

## 16. Exponential Laws

For:

```text
f : X × A ⟶ B
k : X ⟶ A ⇒ B
```

### Beta

```text
uncurry(curry(f))
≡
f
```

### Eta

```text
curry(uncurry(k))
≡
k
```

These express:

```text
Hom(X × A, B)
≅
Hom(X, A ⇒ B)
```

---

## 17. Congruence

Definitional equality is preserved by every core constructor.

If:

```text
f ≡ f'
g ≡ g'
```

then, when well typed:

```text
f >>> g ≡ f' >>> g'
pair(f, g) ≡ pair(f', g')
case(f, g) ≡ case(f', g')
curry(f) ≡ curry(f')
```

---

## 18. Equality Does Not Include User or Model Laws

The kernel does not know:

- Arithmetic equations
- Collection equations
- Domain equations
- User rewrite rules
- Runtime implementation identities
- Model-specific observational equivalences

Such equalities require:

- Explicit proof evidence
- A quotient theory
- A separate model-relative equivalence
- Or a visible trust boundary

They do not alter Phase 0 definitional equality.

---

## 19. Sound Simplification

The implementation may expose a directed simplifier.

Representative rules include:

```text
(f >>> g) >>> h
→
f >>> (g >>> h)
```

```text
id >>> f → f
f >>> id → f
```

```text
pair(f, g) >>> first → f
pair(f, g) >>> second → g
```

```text
left >>> case(f, g) → f
right >>> case(f, g) → g
```

```text
pair(h >>> first, h >>> second)
→
h
```

```text
case(left >>> h, right >>> h)
→
h
```

Canonical exponential beta and eta patterns may also reduce.

Any morphism:

```text
A ⟶ Unit
```

may simplify to:

```text
discard[A]
```

Any morphism:

```text
Never ⟶ A
```

may simplify to:

```text
absurd[A]
```

The simplifier must be:

- Type preserving
- Sound
- Deterministic
- Generator opaque
- Free of model-specific equations
- Free of implicit structural isomorphism insertion

The simplifier is not the equality decision procedure.

---

## 20. Definitional-Equality Decision Procedure

Definitional equality is decided using saturated focusing for the corresponding simply typed lambda calculus with:

- Atomic types
- Unit
- Empty type
- Products
- Sums
- Function types
- Typed opaque constants

Conceptually:

```text
checked categorical morphism
    ↓ translation
typed equality term
    ↓ focusing and saturation
focused saturated form
    ↓ verified comparison
equal / not equal
```

The equality representation is private.

It does not replace the categorical IR.

The procedure must decide exactly the equality generated by Sections 12 through 17.

---

## 21. Equality Proof Requirements

Lean 4 must machine-check:

- Typing of the equality calculus
- Translation from categorical morphisms
- Preservation of typing
- Preservation and reflection of equality
- Termination of focusing
- Termination of saturation
- Soundness
- Completeness
- Correct comparison of focused saturated forms
- Correct treatment of opaque constants

The shipped Rust implementation must be connected to the verified algorithm.

---

## 22. Syntactic Category

For a fixed signature `Σ`, define a category `CΣ` where:

- Objects are well-formed Phase 0 objects.
- Morphisms from `A` to `B` are checked morphisms `A ⟶ B` modulo definitional equality.
- Identity is represented by `id[A]`.
- Composition is represented by `>>>`.

Well-definedness and category laws must be proved.

The full universal-property construction is specified in [[Projects/CategoryLanguage/Metatheory and Categorical Semantics|Metatheory and Categorical Semantics]].

---

## 23. Abstract Models

An abstract model consists of:

- A bicartesian closed category `D`
- An interpretation of each base object
- An interpretation of each generator
- Strict preservation of the chosen Phase 0 structure

The free-category theorem induces a unique interpretation functor:

```text
⟦-⟧ : CΣ → D
```

This is the mathematical semantics of the core.

---

## 24. Executable Runtime Models

The Rust interpreter implements one executable model family.

The interpreter owns runtime structure for:

- Unit
- Products
- Coproducts
- Functions

A supplied runtime model owns:

- Opaque base-object payloads
- Generator callbacks

Runtime values remain tagged by resolved core objects.

Generator inputs and outputs are dynamically checked against their declarations.

Violations are `ModelFault`s.

---

## 25. Closed-Program Evaluation

A closed program has type:

```text
p : Unit ⟶ A
```

Evaluation proceeds:

```text
explicit term
    ↓ check
checked morphism
    ↓ optional sound simplification
runtime interpretation
    ↓ apply to Unit
runtime value of A
```

Checking, simplification, equality, abstract interpretation, and runtime execution are distinct operations.

---

## 26. Examples

### Boolean negation

```text
not =
    case(
        right[Unit, Unit],
        left[Unit, Unit]
    )
```

Then:

```text
false >>> not
```

simplifies to `true`, and:

```text
true >>> not
```

simplifies to `false`.

### Opaque arithmetic

Given:

```text
two   : Unit ⟶ Number
three : Unit ⟶ Number
add   : Number × Number ⟶ Number
```

define:

```text
pair(two, three) >>> add
```

The core equality theory does not reduce this to a numeric literal.

A runtime model may evaluate it to `5`.

### Invalid composition

Given:

```text
f : A ⟶ B
g : C ⟶ D
```

```text
f >>> g
```

is rejected unless `B` and `C` are structurally equal.

No automatic canonical isomorphism is inserted.

---

## 27. Phase 0 Completion Criteria

Phase 0 is complete when:

- Signatures are resolved and immutable.
- Every object form is represented.
- Every term constructor is represented.
- Potentially ill-typed terms can be constructed.
- Every typing rule is implemented.
- Checked terms produce trusted morphisms.
- Invalid composition is rejected.
- Structural object equality is implemented.
- Sound simplification is implemented.
- Complete equality is implemented.
- Equality termination, soundness, and completeness are machine-checked.
- The syntactic category is constructed in Lean.
- The bicartesian-closed universal properties are proved.
- The free-category theorem is proved.
- Abstract interpretation is defined as the induced functor.
- The Rust equality implementation is connected to the verified procedure.
- Closed programs execute in at least one runtime model.
- Runtime contract violations are explicit model faults.
- Core IR is inspectable.
- No source parser, variables, recursion, effects, resources, or source polymorphism are required.
